blindSummary:
The territory is an autonomous constituent country within a distant overseas kingdom. It must recognise same-sex marriages lawfully performed in the metropolitan state (a 2007 ruling of the kingdom's highest court) but has no local marriage equality; the economy is tourism-dependent; there is no legal gender recognition.

Because direct territory-specific documentation is thin, this record rests substantially on the metropolitan state's legal and social evidence base, of which the territory's framework is an inheritance.
blindOutOfScope: A constituent territory of a distant metropolitan state; local deviations are noted in the summary.
blindSourceSummaries: A world-pride host-city safety and travel page (about the metropolitan state, included here as regional context): entry/border procedures, passport-carrying rules of the regional visa-free area, main-airport logistics, taxi safety and general city caution, with a dedicated section for transgender and non-binary visitors.

International LGBT-rights organisation overview of the metropolitan state (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal, marriage and adoption available, legal gender recognition possible but still requires an expert letter from a medical professional; non-binary 'X' marker only via a court procedure taking 3-9 months; the self-ID gender law was withdrawn by the metropolitan government in July 2025. Included as context because the territory's legal framework is tied to the metropolitan state's as a constituent part of the same overseas kingdom.

The territory's official tourism website LGBT-vacations page: markets the island under a cheerful island-brand slogan as welcoming to all visitors, with nearly 100 nationalities living together; general tourism promotion with an LGBT-specific landing page.

Official tourism-site news item: the island voted to introduce LGBT civil unions, the first such decision by an island in the region - official promotion of the territory's LGBT-inclusive development.

Independent gay-travel culture report (2017): describes gay life in the territory as part of a tolerant and mostly open society - a group of three small neighbouring islands off the same coast within the same overseas kingdom, characterised as quiet niches of gay-friendliness; travel-oriented first-person perspective.

News-agency report carried by a web portal (Sept 2016): the island's parliament voted 11-5 (4 abstentions) to grant same-sex couples the right to register unions and receive the benefits granted to married people (spousal pension, emergency medical decisions); previously couples married in the metropolitan state could have their certificates recognised; one parliamentarian noted many islanders oppose same-sex unions on religious and cultural grounds.
